name: Wendy Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am junior on a yoghurt filling machine at a dairy, feeding pots, checking weight and pressing foil lids for leaks. I finished secondary school and am still slow at the heat changeover, so Rosa the line leader watches the first batch with me. The cold room makes the early shift feel longer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is happening at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Paulo does plumbing jobs, and we have two school-age children, a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved. My dairy pay is low, his bookings vary, and only a few similar plants are nearby. I use AI now and then for shopping lists, but I try a new work control only after watching it run safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the yoghurt crew that a report can be quick, but a loose foil lid still needs someone at the filler. I use AI now and then for shopping lists, not for releasing food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the dairy to keep selling yoghurt, yet my junior pay is small beside our mortgage and Paulo’s plumbing van costs. We have two children and less than a month saved, so one cancelled week would hurt us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep feeding pots and checking lid seals, then ask Rosa the line leader to show me one more changeover. From a full paid week I would put only the surplus after mortgage and food into a new emergency transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary bills, even if AI stays modest. An empty pay packet is harder than a cold dairy shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you test a lid before a batch goes out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I press around the edge and turn the pot to see whether foil lifts at one corner. If it does, Rosa and I stop the filler and check heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a full week always leave a surplus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, Paulo’s plumbing receipts vary and school costs arrive without warning. I would record the real remainder before transferring any new money.

think: My **junior pay** and variable plumbing income leave a thin margin.
Less than **one month saved** makes a cancelled week serious.
do: Keep feeding **yoghurt pots** and checking foil seals.
Learn another **changeover** from Rosa on the current line.
Transfer **new wage surplus** after mortgage and food when a full week allows.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary bills despite little AI change.

fieldNote: Wendy sees a secure product but remains pressed by **low pay** and thin savings.
Her extra transfer depends on **actual fresh wages**, with variable household plumbing income treated honestly.

Save fresh pay only when mortgage and food leave a surplus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say quicker orders are fine if the dairy keeps paid people who know when a seal fails. Companies should teach workers on the floor before they buy a tray robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other hall already has a packer that can stack pots, and my own junior hours could be first to shrink. Paulo’s plumbing jobs are uneven; his income would not cover the mortgage if the dairy cut two days from my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my filler shift and ask Rosa to show me the packer after it has run safely for a full week. If the plant offers paid guarded practice, I would learn its controls; if two rosters cut my hours, we would stop weekend takeaways and I would check posted nearby food-line jobs at bill-covering pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage, but I can learn from a real run. I do not want a video to be called training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Rosa to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where the arm stops when a pot breaks and how she clears a jam with the power isolated. I would not reach past a guard to save a batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have less than a month saved and only a few factories nearby. I need an offered paid place at work before I practise controls.

I would keep **seal checks** in the paid filler routine.

Cut **weekend takeaways** after two reduced rosters.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours, with a practical response.

fieldNote: Her steady style waits for **one proven week** and an offered paid place before learning controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift thinking AI could change orders in 2028 when I am forty five, and capable robots might handle our pots around 2031 when I am forty eight. We should know who checks the food before any staff cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the junior filler shifts to fall once robots seal and pack reliably. Paulo’s plumbing bookings may also be hit later, and our few weeks saved cannot carry the mortgage if both incomes weaken; I wake up counting bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cut the family trip and stop optional purchases now, then ask for the dairy’s written staffing plan. If my paid hours go, I would apply only to a posted reachable food-factory job with bill-covering wages and safe paid instruction; if none appears, I would ask family for temporary help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make calls, but I cannot make a month of wages appear before the mortgage date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What checks would a robot line still need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person must test the lid seal and record the batch before it leaves the dairy. I would want a guarded test that shows what happens when the foil tears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the family could help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister could watch the children while I attended an offered paid practical place. I would not ask her to cover a permanent wage gap.

I would require **seal tests** before any robot line releases food.
think: I expect **junior filler hours** to shrink after physical robots arrive.
Our **few weeks saved** and uncertain plumbing income cannot bridge a long mortgage gap.
do: Cut the **family trip** and optional purchases now.

feel: **Alarmed** by expected large wage loss and sleepless bill counting.

fieldNote: Wendy expects **large hour loss** and says the bills wake her at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am forty eight, and capable filler robots follow around 2034 when I am fifty one. Five years is enough to see which line truly works before changing my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still need the dairy wage at fifty one because our mortgage does not vanish on a robot calendar. I would be open to a different machine after a real demonstration, but only if a paid place and a job exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the filler shifts and put new surplus from each full month into our emergency account. If the dairy offers a fully funded food-machine maintenance course on paid time with a workshop place and a posted nearby bill-covering job, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; otherwise I would stay on the filler while it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a longer warning lets us build some cash and check a real route. I want a machine I can stop, not a certificate that cannot pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical maintenance involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn to isolate the heat sealer and replace a worn belt with a qualified fitter beside me. Rosa could show me the ordinary changeover, but this is a different job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for an unpaid course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Paulo and I cannot lose dairy wages for study days. The course funding and paid hours must be written down before I enrol.

I would distinguish **2031 ordering AI** from 2034 physical filler robots.
think: The **mortgage** still needs my dairy wage at fifty one.

fieldNote: Wendy treats **maintenance** as a separate occupation requiring practical instruction, not an informal filler briefing.

steps.text: Keep paid filler shifts and save new surplus after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir and the shift that thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am fifty three, while capable filler robots follow around 2039 when I am fifty six. Thirteen years gives families time to prepare if wages keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children may be older by then, but I cannot assume the mortgage or Paulo’s uneven plumbing income will be solved. I may still need my lower-paid dairy shift, and less than a month saved now makes the first years important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the paid filling shift and record what each full month truly leaves after bills. In the first year after 2036, if I still work there, I would compare the rota with posted local jobs; after two reduced months I would apply only to a reachable bill-covering role with safe paid instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money now and uncertain hours later. A long warning helps only while the pay packet is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the children’s studies because of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask them to learn a trade and be good with people, but I would not choose their courses from one forecast. They still need school now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you try a new control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A full-week safe run, an offered paid practice place and someone qualified to show the stop. A new tablet alone would not make the dairy shift secure.

I would ask families to prepare while **paid work** still exists.
think: My **dairy wage** may still be needed at fifty six.
The **mortgage** and uneven plumbing income remain real today.
do: Keep the **paid filler shift** and record monthly surplus now.

feel: **Anxious** about current bills and future shift cuts.

fieldNote: Her ten-year answer preserves **today’s thin margin** rather than assuming children or the mortgage solve themselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because dairy robots could take junior filler hours by 2031 while the mortgage and school costs keep arriving. Paid practical training and a posted local job with enough wage to cover bills would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a yoghurt lid when nobody is paid to stand beside the filler. A leaking pot cannot be put back together after it reaches a child’s lunch.

headlineQuote: A leaking pot cannot be put back together after it reaches a child’s lunch.
portrait: **Wendy**, 43, is a junior dairy filler operator with secondary schooling and a careful, practical approach to new controls.
Her **low pay**, variable plumbing income, mortgage, two children, thin savings and few nearby plants make lost hours costly.
She uses AI **occasionally** at home, then waits for safe production proof and offered paid practice before learning factory controls.
Her **existing money pressure** stays anxious in the plateau; expected major hours loss makes the fast case alarming.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut Wendy’s junior dairy hours around 2031 while household mortgage costs continue.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** and a posted reachable job with enough wage for household bills would help.
